seo.title: Karmic tail 3 4 10 compatibility: the couple of doubles
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 4 10 compatibility appears only when both partners have the personal tail 15-20-5. What the Empress, the Emperor and the Wheel mean for two.

title: Karmic tail 3-4-10 in compatibility: a home, a throne and a wheel for two
short: The 3-4-10 tail never belongs to one person, and it does not form between just anyone: it appears only in a couple where both partners have the same personal tail, 15-20-5. Two identical triples, added together, make a new one. The Empress at the entry to the task is a shared wish for a home where there is enough of everything. The Emperor in the middle is an order in which both rule and both obey. The Wheel of Fortune in the main task is the skill of taking the turns of time together, without trying to stop them.

sections.h2: What the 3-4-10 tail means: a couple made of doubles
paragraphs: The first oddity is the middle. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is always the sum of its ends, the entry and the main task. For the ends 3 and 10 that gives 13, Death. Here the middle is 4, the Emperor. There is no mistake: in a couple every point is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, and the couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles, not of the ends. That is why 3-4-10 exists only for two.

The second oddity is stronger. The site's engine went through the combinations of dates: the couple's tail 3-4-10 comes from one single combination, 15-20-5 + 15-20-5, in a hundred per cent of such couples. A 3-4-10 couple is always two people with the same personal tail.
Add their tails together and each card meets its double:

ul: **The Hierophant + the Hierophant:** 5 + 5 = 10, the Wheel of Fortune.

paragraphs: The couple does not continue the personal tails; it doubles them, and doubling produces different cards. What 15-20-5 means for each partner alone is the subject of the personal tail. What matters here is something else: in a couple the same numbers sound differently.

The third clue is frequency. 15-20-5 is the most common of the 26 personal tails: by our own count with the same engine, it belongs to 10.06% of all dates from 1900 to 2026, roughly one person in ten. Two such people end up in one couple about once in a hundred — a tenth of a tenth. The engine says the same: the 3-4-10 tail occurs in about one couple in 99 (1.013%), 37th place out of 97 couple tails. And only two of the 97 couple tails are built entirely from two identical personal tails: 3-4-10 and 3-16-22. Ours is almost six times more common.

The fourth clue is the centre. Every person with the 15-20-5 tail has the Wheel of Fortune at the centre of the chart, without exception. So the couple's main task, 10, is the very card each of the two carries at the centre of their own matrix. And the couple's centre is 10 + 10 = 20, Judgement, again in every such couple. **What each partner carries inside becomes the couple's task.**
The partners share the tail and the centre; the other points of their two charts can be anything. So they are doubles by tail, not by character.

sections.h2: A worked example: two people born on 17.01.1976
paragraphs: The clearest case is two people with the same date of birth, 17 January 1976. The day, 17, is the Star; the month, 1, is the Magician; the year, 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5, is the Hierophant. The karmic task at the bottom of the chart: 17 + 1 + 5 = 23 → 5. The centre: 17 + 1 + 5 + 5 = 28 → 10. The entry of the tail: 5 + 10 = 15; the middle: 15 + 5 = 20. Each of them has the personal tail 15-20-5.
Now the couple: the matching points of the two charts are added.

The couple's centre is 10 + 10 = 20, Judgement. The couple's values in this example are 6, the Lovers. In real life partners with the 3-4-10 tail usually have different dates: what they share is the personal tail and the centre, not the birthday.

sections.h2: Philemon and Baucis: "the whole family are but two"
paragraphs: Their names long ago became a byword for a devoted old couple, but Ovid's story is far more exact than that reputation. "Metamorphoses", Book VIII. At a feast in the house of the river god Achelous, a guest, Pirithous, "a despiser of the Gods", laughs at tales of transformation: fiction, he says — the gods cannot give and take away shapes. Old Lelex answers with a story he says he checked himself: "I, myself, have seen the spot."

On the Phrygian hills an oak and a lime tree stand side by side inside a low wall. Nearby lies a marsh — "a standing water, formerly habitable ground". Jupiter and Mercury came here in human form. "To a thousand houses did they go, asking for lodging and for rest. A thousand houses did the bolts fasten against them." One took them in, a small one, thatched with straw and marsh reeds. In it lived Baucis and Philemon, "of a like age": they were united in that cottage when young, and in it they grew old together. "It matters not, whether you ask for the masters there, or for the servants; the whole family are but two; the same persons both obey and command."

Then Ovid writes the supper in close, homely detail. Baucis blows yesterday's embers into flame with her old breath, Philemon lifts a smoked side of bacon down from the beam, the table has a short leg and they prop it with a potsherd. The wine in the bowl rises by itself; the old people take fright and beg pardon for their poor table. They have a single goose, the guardian of the cottage. They chase it to kill it for their guests, and the goose takes refuge with the gods themselves. The gods reveal who they are: the impious neighbourhood will be punished, and the hosts are told to climb the mountain with them — "go together". An arrow's flight short of the summit, the old people look back and see that everything has sunk under water except their cottage. And while they weep for their neighbours, the cottage "was changed into a temple": columns rise where the forked stakes stood, the thatch turns into a golden roof, the earth into marble.

Jupiter asks what they wish for. Philemon exchanged a few words with Baucis and announced their "common judgement": to be priests and guard the temple, and since their years were passed in harmony, to let the same hour take both of them. And so it was. One day, very old, they stood by the temple steps telling the story of the place — and Baucis saw Philemon putting out leaves, and Philemon saw the same in Baucis. Before the leaves closed over their faces, they managed to say goodbye to each other — at the same moment.

Read the Latin closely and the story turns out to have a single vocabulary. Baucis and Philemon are equal in age (parili aetate). The household is "two" (duo), and in it "the same persons" (idem) command and obey. The cottage is small "even for two owners". They ask for "the same" hour (hora eadem). They say goodbye "together", and together the leaves cover their faces (simul, simul). And in the last lines Ovid twice calls them by the word geminus, "twin, paired": the treetop grows over their "twin faces", and the locals point to two neighbouring trunks "from a twin body". **The arithmetic of the tail writes the 3-4-10 couple the same way: two of a kind.** Quotations from Ovid follow H. T. Riley's prose translation (1893); where Riley loses the Latin word, the literal meaning is ours.

The three cards of the tail each have their place in this story. The Empress is the supper made from the last of everything and the bowl that fills itself. The Emperor is the household where two both command and obey, and the potsherd under the short table leg. The Wheel of Fortune is the cottage turned into a temple and the request for one hour for two. And Judgement, from the couple's centre, sounds in the word Ovid uses for their answer to the gods: a common judgement.

sections.h2: The Empress, entry to the task: a table they apologise for
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's reading, the entry to the couple's tail is what the two want together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also turn into resistance. In the 3-4-10 couple this point holds the Empress. Waite calls her "universal fecundity". Wen sees in her a gift for turning relationships between people into success and harmony: "She produces. She makes things happen".

The common language of such couples is a home where there is enough of everything and enough for everyone. A kitchen where something is always cooking. A country house where both of them keep bringing friends. A shared business, a renovation discussed like a serial novel, talk about living somewhere closer to the land. Agreeing comes easily to them because they want the same thing. Philemon and Baucis each know their part of the supper: she fans the fire and strips the cabbage he gathered in his garden, he takes the bacon down from the beam, and the conversation with the guests never stops.

Ovid ends his list of dishes with a line worth reading him for. Nuts, dates, plums, apples, grapes, a white honeycomb in the middle — "above all, there are welcome looks, and no indifferent and niggardly feelings". The entry to this couple's task is not wealth but generosity with whatever there is.

The resistance hides in the same scene. As soon as the wine in the bowl starts rising by itself, the hosts take fright and "entreat pardon for their entertainment, and their want of preparation". And they rush to catch their last goose, "the guardian of their little cottage", so that the table will be worthier. The wish for a full house easily turns into shame at a house that is not full: spending the reserve on a celebration like everyone else's, saying yes to the relatives' expectations, measuring one's own table against others'. Lisovskaya names exactly this in the minus of the Empress in a couple: getting out from under the influence of a mother and relatives, surviving feast and famine, not looking down on whoever is earning less at the moment. In Ovid the gods do not let them kill the goose. **A full table is not worth the guardian of the house.**

And one more subtlety. What frightens the old people is not poverty — they are used to it — but abundance that came by itself. A couple whose language is "we'll do it all ourselves" is wary of what it has not earned: help, luck, a gift. It is curious that Waite puts the words "increase, abundance, superfluity" in the reversed Wheel of Fortune. The bowl that fills itself is the Wheel's first appearance, already at the entry to the task.

sections.h2: The Emperor, middle of the task: "the same persons both obey and command"
paragraphs: The middle of the couple's tail, in our reading, shows how the two travel from the shared wish to the main task: what they do and what they go through. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own — it only adds to the main task — so this reading is the product's adaptation.

In the 3-4-10 couple the middle holds the Emperor, and he is made of two Judgements: two people with one tail build one state. Waite gives the Emperor the words "stability, power, protection, realization". Wen calls four "the number of force and sovereignty". In daily life this means plans for years ahead, a budget in a spreadsheet, savings for a rainy day, the rule "measure twice, cut once", shared duties, the habit of covering for each other. Lisovskaya describes the minus too: rules that later get in the way, control and decisions made for everyone, coldness, a life in which they "never go anywhere", and the struggle for leadership.

For doubles, the struggle for leadership is a special one. Both know "the right way", and know it in the same way, so for a long time they agree on everything — until the first question of "who decides". Then it turns out there is one throne and two people who know how to sit on it.

Ovid's answer is more exact than any advice: "the whole family are but two; the same persons both obey and command". Not "one commands, the other obeys", and not "nobody commands", but both — in turn and by subject. The strong version of the middle looks ordinary. One leads on holiday, the other on the renovation, the budget is run together, but the last word on each item belongs to whoever is responsible for it. And each knows how to obey in the other's zone as calmly as to command in their own.

One more detail from the same scene, small and precise. "The third leg of the table is too short; a potsherd, placed beneath, makes it equal." **This couple's order at its best is a potsherd under a wobbly leg, not a new table.** The rules are not carved in stone: they are propped up and adjusted when the table rocks.

Here the missing card comes to mind. In a personal matrix with these ends, Death would stand in the middle — the card of the end of a stage and the change of form. In the couple, a throne stands in its place. The 3-4-10 couple goes through the middle not by ending the old but by building and keeping. There is strength in that, and a risk too: keeping a form that is due to change — a rule that has outlived its reason, a family ritual that has long stopped pleasing anyone.

Goethe showed what the Emperor looks like without the Empress. In the second part of "Faust" the cottage of Philemon and Baucis stands on a shore granted to Faust by the emperor, der Kaiser. Faust has won the land from the sea and built a palace, yet he has no peace: "these few trees, not mine, spoil my possession of the world". And further: "we are tormented most when, amid our riches, we feel what we lack". Mephistopheles "clears" the plot, the cottage burns, the old couple die of fright, and Faust mutters: "I wanted exchange, not robbery". (Lines from "Faust" are our translation.) For the 3-4-10 couple this is a warning about the minus of the middle: a plan built for the sake of the home begins to demand that the home fit into it.

sections.h2: The Wheel of Fortune, main task: turning together
paragraphs: The main task, in Lisovskaya's reading, is the couple's chief trials, and it is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what has to be learned. In the 3-4-10 couple it is the Wheel of Fortune, for Lisovskaya the energy of cycles. Rises and crises follow one another, and the thing to fight is not the change itself but the way the couple goes through it.

Ovid opens the story with the Wheel without naming it: "a standing water, formerly habitable ground". Waite describes the Wheel in a similar way: "the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and the flux of human life". At the climax the Wheel makes its turn: the cottage "vertitur in templum", literally "is turned into a temple". Neither of the two controls it. They are told "go together", and Ovid notes: "They both obeyed".

Why is it the Wheel that stands as the main task for doubles? Wen compares the Wheel to the unit circle of trigonometry, to sine and cosine, "oscillations between zeniths and nadirs". What follows is our reading. Two identical waves in the same phase add up: the peaks get higher and the troughs deeper. In a couple with identical tails the highs and lows can come at the same time: both get tired in the same week, both fall silent on the same evening, and there is no one to hold on while the other falls. Lisovskaya describes the minus of the Wheel in a couple as a swing between silence and conflict, mood swings, the feeling of not being heard, the habit of blaming fate and each other, problems left to drift.

The Emperor in the middle answers this in his own way — he builds a dam. A cushion of money, a schedule, rules for a crisis: all of this is right until the dam turns into a bolt. "A thousand houses did the bolts fasten against them" — that is Ovid's picture of a neighbourhood that did not open the door when change — in our reading — knocked in the shape of weary travellers. For the Wheel, Lisovskaya advises exactly the opposite of a bolt: not closing up on each other, inviting friends, taking up new things, sometimes letting go of control.

Ovid hid the main key to the Wheel in his very first description of the couple: "by owning their poverty, they rendered it light", bearing it without resentment (paupertatemque fatendo effecere levem nec iniqua mente ferendo). Not hiding it, not dressing it up — owning it. For the 3-4-10 couple this is the hardest part, because the Emperor's order knows how to pretend that everything is under control. **To name the bottom of the wheel aloud — "we have nothing right now", "I feel bad right now" — is already to be halfway through it.** Lisovskaya puts the Wheel's tasks just as simply: speak sincerely, look for solutions instead of complaints, accept the partner with their flaws.

And the last thing Ovid says about the Wheel is the request itself. Two people to whom a god offers anything ask neither for riches nor for time to stop. They ask for the same hour for both. The Wheel's task for doubles is not to hold the rim still, but to know where the other is on it right now, and not to lose their shared time.

Jonathan Swift retold the myth in English in 1706, with his own irony: the travellers became two saintly hermits, Phrygia a village in Kent, the cottage a church. His best find is the kitchen roasting-jack. The wooden mechanism that used to turn the roast follows the chimney as it grows into a steeple, gains new inner wheels, and "the number made the motion slower": now it "hardly moves an inch an hour". The jack has become the church clock — and still cries out at noon, "warning the cook-maid not to burn / That roast meat which it cannot turn". It is an exact picture of the 3-4-10 minus: the living wheel of the home, fitted into the order, starts only to count time and to remind, and no longer knows how to turn.

The strong version is in Ovid's last scene. Baucis saw Philemon putting out leaves, and Philemon saw the same in Baucis. The line is built as a mirror: frondere Philemona Baucis, / Baucida conspexit senior frondere Philemon. In the turn, each is the first to notice the change in the other and manages to say so while they still can.

sections.h2: Judgement at the couple's centre: "a common judgement"
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the shared atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In every 3-4-10 couple it holds Judgement, 20, and the numbers are simple: each partner has the Wheel at the centre, and 10 + 10 = 20. Judgement also stands in the middle of each partner's personal tail — a coincidence of numbers; in meaning these are different points.

Lisovskaya links Judgement in a couple to family and lineage. In the plus the atmosphere is cosy: they orient themselves by each other in everything, behave as equals and know how to give way, forgive mistakes, support each other even when the other is wrong. In the minus there is closedness towards each other, blame without owning one's own share, sudden cooling, refusal of help, and the most telling sign: neither can say what they feel and what they dislike.

In Ovid the word that matters stands right in the middle of the scene. Philemon, "having spoken a few words to Baucis", reveals to the gods their common decision — iudicium commune. Iudicium in Latin is exactly judgement: an opinion, a decision, a verdict (Riley renders it "joint request"). Waite puts "deliberation, decision, sentence" in the divinatory list of Judgement. Wen writes of this card: "All evidence has been made available to the Seeker and the Seeker has rendered his or her judgment. It does not end there, however".

The atmosphere of the 3-4-10 couple is an inner court for two. Decisions come quickly, a few words are enough because they think alike, and what reaches the outside world is a finished "we've decided". That is lovely as long as both voices are heard in those few words. The minus begins when the deliberation shrinks to one: one passes the verdict and the other learns of it along with the guests. Or both pass judgement on a third — a relative, a friend — without once asking themselves. Waite describes Judgement as a summons that is "heard and answered from within". **In the strong version the couple's shared court is not a tribunal but the moment when two people honestly hear the same thing and answer together.**

sections.h2: The couple's values: the Lovers or the Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. In 3-4-10 couples there are two options: 6, the Lovers, in 55.2%, and 15, the Devil, in 44.8%. It is curious that the Devil, which vanished from the tail in the addition (15 + 15 became the Empress), returns in the values of almost half of these couples.

The Lovers are the union as a choice, made and repeated. "United in their youthful years in that cottage, and in it, they grew old together": Ovid does not write that it was easy; he writes that they chose one place and one person. For doubles this is the main question of values: are they together because they choose each other, or because things happened to match?

The Devil is the union as attachment. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the fifteenth energy with the thought that nobody belongs to anybody. Swift, without meaning to, drew the minus of this value in his last lines. His Baucis and Philemon became two yews in the churchyard, and when the parson cut one down to mend his barn, the other tree "died a-top, was stunted". Swift is joking, but a couple with the Devil in its values recognises its own fear in the joke: alone, neither can go on. The strong version is attachment in which each keeps a root of their own.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 3-4-10 tail
paragraphs: A couple's tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast but a pattern in which two people can recognise their habits. In its strong version 3-4-10 looks like this:

ul: **Name the bottom of the wheel aloud.** Owned poverty becomes light — in Ovid, literally.
**Share the throne by zones.** In each matter one leads and the other obeys, and in the next it is the other way round.
**Mend the order with a potsherd.** Review the rules in small steps and often, without waiting for the table to fall.
**Don't chase the last goose.** Don't spend the reserve or sacrifice what guards the house for a table like everyone else's.
**Don't fall in the same phase.** Agree while both are at the top: when one is down, the other holds on.
**Open the door.** Friends, guests, new pursuits, people unlike the two of them: in our reading, the Wheel in Ovid arrives in the shape of strangers on the road.
**Accept what came by itself.** Help and luck — without fear and without apologising for the table.

paragraphs: Lelex ends his story by saying that he himself hung fresh garlands on the branches of the two trees. His story has not a word about the old couple earning their temple by wealth or by great deeds. They owned their poverty, opened the door and decided together. The Wheel turned, and the cottage became a temple without ceasing to be their home.

sections.h2: What comes from the books and what is our reading

ul: The numbers are the site engine's calculation: shares, combinations of personal tails, the couple's centre and values. The frequency of the personal tail 15-20-5 and the comparison with 3-16-22 are our own count with the same engine.

The meaning of the couple's points follows Yuliana Lisovskaya's book "Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost" ("The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility", 2024); the meaning of the middle of the tail is the product's adaptation. Even Lisovskaya has no ready readings of couple tails: the book analyses only two.
Waite and Wen are quoted in the original, from "The Pictorial Key to the Tarot" and "Holistic Tarot".
Ovid — "Metamorphoses", VIII, 611–724, in H. T. Riley's translation; Swift — "Baucis and Philemon"; Goethe — "Faust", Part Two, Act V. The Latin glosses and the lines from Goethe are our translation.
Matching the story to the cards of the tail is our reading, not the teaching of the sources.

intro: Ovid has a couple of whom he says: "the whole family are but two; the same persons both obey and command." Philemon and Baucis spent their lives in a cramped cottage, fed the gods with the last they had, watched the cottage become a temple, and asked for one thing only — a shared hour for the two of them. Their story lays itself out across the three cards of this tail, and the numbers explain why it belongs to a couple of doubles.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3-4-10 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple in which both partners have the personal tail 15-20-5. The entry to the task is the Empress, a shared wish for a home and plenty. The middle is the Emperor, an order in which both know how to lead and how to give way. The main task is the Wheel of Fortune: going through highs and lows together, without hiding them and without trying to stop them.

faq.q: Why is there no 3-4-10 tail in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal chart the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: 3 + 10 = 13. In a couple the middle is the sum of the partners' middles: 20 + 20 = 40 → 4. That is why 3-4-10 is possible only for two.

faq.q: Does a 3-4-10 couple have identical matrices?
faq.a: No. The personal tails (15-20-5) and the centres (10, the Wheel of Fortune) match; the other points of the two charts can differ. Fully identical matrices belong only to people born on the same day, as in the example of 17.01.1976.

The 3-4-10 couple tail has no permutations of the same numbers. With the same ends — the Empress at the entry and the Wheel of Fortune in the main task — there are two more couple tails: with Death in the middle (3-13-10) and with the Fool (3-22-10). The ends are shared, but the road from the home to the turn is different.

faq.q: Is the 3-4-10 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes tasks, not fate: it does not predict events and does not grade the union. The strong side of 3-4-10 is a generous home and the skill of building a shared order; the hard side is the habit of holding on to a form when it is time to turn.

report: The 3-4-10 tail never belongs to one person, and it does not form between just anyone. It appears only where two people share the personal tail 15-20-5, and in the couple each card finds its double: two Devils make the Empress, two Judgements make the Emperor, two Hierophants make the Wheel of Fortune. And the Wheel, which becomes the couple's main task, stands at the centre of each partner's own chart. **What each partner carries inside becomes the couple's task.**

Philemon, "having spoken a few words to Baucis", announces to the gods their "common judgement" — in Latin iudicium commune, literally a shared verdict. This couple's decisions come quickly, a few words are enough, because they think alike. That is lovely as long as both voices are heard in those words. The minus begins when the deliberation shrinks to one, or when neither can say what they feel.

Ovid's last scene is the strong version of the whole tail. Very old, by the temple steps, Baucis saw Philemon putting out leaves, and Philemon saw the same in Baucis. In the turn of the wheel each is the first to notice the change in the other and manages to say so while they still can. The cottage became a temple without ceasing to be their home.

unit.meaning: Your task is to take the turns together: say the hard things aloud and hold each other up when one of you is down.
